title: Trial Specifications Document
text:
1 Introduction
This Trial Specifications Document (TSD) describes the design and technical details of the Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE) of North Pacific swordfish (Xiphias gladius; NSWO), including the operating models, candidate management procedures, and performance metrics used to evaluate them.
The TSD is a living document that will be updated as the MSE progresses to reflect the current state of the analysis.
For more information on the North Pacific Swordfish MSE process see the project homepage.

title: Trial Specifications Document
text:
1.1 About the NSWO MSE
The NSWO MSE is built and maintained by Blue Matter Science using the openMSE framework.
The analysis is fully reproducible, and all materials are available in the associated GitHub repository.

title: 2  Operating Models
text:
2.1 OM Conditioning
The 2023 ISC stock assessment of North Pacific swordfish, which was fitted with Stock Synthesis 3 (SS3; Methot and Wetzel (2013)), was used to generate the operating models (OMs).
The assessment is a two-sex model with 4 quarterly time steps per year, covering 1975–2021. It includes 19 fishing fleets and 8 CPUE indices (Figure 2.1; Table 2.1). Steepness of the Beverton-Holt stock-recruitment relationship is fixed at 0.9. See the assessment report for further details on the assessment structure and assumptions.
The OMs were constructed by importing the SS3 output of each assessment run, available from the WCNPOSWO-2023 repository, into the North Pacific swordfish MSE framework.
Figure 2.1: Overview of the data used in the 2023 base case stock assessment.

title: 2  Operating Models
text:
2.1.1 Catch Units
In the assessment, the catch of 8 of the 19 fishing fleets is in numbers of fish (thousands), and the catch of the remaining fleets is in biomass (t). Because the total allowable catch (TAC) management advice produced by the candidate management procedures (CMPs) is in units of biomass (tons), the catch of every fleet was imported in biomass, using the catch biomass predicted by SS3 for the fleets with catch in numbers.

2.1.2 Fleet Structure
To reduce run time, the 19 fishing fleets were combined into a single fleet in the operating models. The combined fleet reproduces the historical fishing mortality-at-age of the individual fleets, with selectivity, retention, and weight-at-age weighted by the fishing mortality of each fleet. This results in exactly the same fishery and population dynamics as an operating model that includes the 19 fleet structure. In the projection period, the relative contribution of each fleet (i.e., TAC allocation) is therefore assumed to be fixed at its recent pattern.







Figure 2.2: Total annual catch data in the base case OM.





2.1.3 Indices of Abundance
Table 2.1 lists the CPUE indices in the assessment. The Japanese longline indices (Area 1 and Area 2; both split into an Early and Late phase) were selected to be used by the CMPs.
The index-based CMPs use the two that continue to the terminal year (S2 and S4; Figure 2.3). The surplus production CMPs also use the earlier Japanese longline series (S1 and S3; see Chapter 5).
Two of the indices (S5 and S8) were not fitted in the base case assessment (lambda = 0), and therefore were not included in the data passed to the CMPs.
S6, an index of recruitment, was also not used by the CMPs. This index has a higher CV than the Japanese longline indices, and as it does not track the adult population it did not provide any additional information that could improve the performance of the CMPs.

title: 2  Operating Models
text:
2.2 Base Case and Sensitivity OMs

2.2.1 OMs Included in the MSE
The 2023 assessment included sensitivity runs with alternative life-history parameters (natural mortality, steepness, growth, and maturity), catch assumptions, model settings, and CPUE indices. OMs were constructed from the base case and the 9 sensitivity runs with alternative life-history parameters (Table 2.2; Table 2.3). The other sensitivity runs are not currently included in the MSE.
Three of these runs are not included in the MSE:


Run 03 (steepness 0.70): the control file sets steepness to 0.70, but the starter file initialises the parameters from the base case parameter file, where steepness is 0.9. Because steepness is fixed, the fitted model has steepness of 0.9 and the SS3 output is identical to the base case, so the run does not represent the steepness sensitivity.

Runs 05 (steepness 0.99) and 06 (maximum size 10% larger): the SS3 fits estimate an implausibly large stock, with ln(R0) of 32.37 and 35.06 compared with 6.84 in the base case, and unfished spawning biomass of the order of \(10^{16}\) and \(10^{17}\) t. The stock in these OMs is therefore effectively unfished and unaffected by the catch.

The CMPs are tuned on the base case OM (Section 5.7) and their robustness is evaluated on the 6 included sensitivity OMs.

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.1 Management Cycle and Data Lag
Each operating model has 100 independent simulations with stochastic samples of the log-normally distributed recruitment deviations, the observation error for the indices of abundance, and the catches in the initial projection years (see below).
The projection period covers 2022–2057, with 4 quarterly time steps per year.
The MSE assumes that the first TAC generated by the CMPs will apply in 2028, with a 3-year management cycle and a 2-year data lag.
This means that the TAC for 2028 is calculated in 2027 using data up to 2025, and the TAC is then updated every 3 years (Table 3.1).
The TAC is set for each calendar year and applies to the total catch of all fleets. Within each year, the TAC is split among the quarters in proportion to the seasonal distribution of the catch over the last 5 historical years.

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.2 Initial Projection Years
The historical period of the OMs ends in 2021, the terminal year of the assessment. Because the first TAC generated by the CMPs will apply in 2028, the first 6 years of the projection period (2022–2027) are an extension of the historical period rather than years managed by the CMPs.
The catches in these interim years combine reported catches, where they are available, with assumed catches based on the recent catches of each fleet (all in t):


Reported catches are available for F3_US_WCNPO_LL_shallow_late and F9_US_WCNPO_LL_deep in 2022–2025, and for F19_WCPFC in 2022–2024.
The catches of F3 and F9 are reported in numbers of fish and are converted to biomass with the mean weight of the catch of each fleet in the last five assessment years.


Assumed catches are used for all other fleets and years, including all fleets in 2026–2027 and F19_WCPFC in 2025.
For each fleet, the catch is drawn from a lognormal distribution with the mean and coefficient of variation (CV) of the fleet’s catch over its last five years with catch data, truncated at the maximum catch over its last ten years. These catches are the historical catches of the OM (the catch biomass estimated in the corresponding SS3 run, which the OM reproduces) followed by any reported catches, so for most fleets they are the catches in 2017–2021.


The catches of the individual fleets are then combined into the total catch in each year (Table 3.2).

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.3 Recruitment Deviations
Recruitment deviations are generated as autocorrelated, bias-corrected log-normal deviates around the stock-recruit relationship. For a given simulation, the (log-scale) deviation in year \(y\) is calculated as:
\[
\varepsilon_y \sim \text{TruncNormal}(\mu, \sigma_R,\ \pm 3\sigma_R)
\]
\[
x_y = \rho\, x_{y-1} + \varepsilon_y \sqrt{1-\rho^2}
\]
\[
\text{RecDev}_y = \exp(x_y)
\]
where \(\sigma_R\) is the recruitment deviation standard deviation, \(\rho\) is the lag-1 autocorrelation, and \(\mu = -0.5\sigma_R^2(1-\rho)/\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\) is a bias-correction term so that \(E[\text{RecDev}_y] = 1\) on the natural scale. Deviations are truncated at \(\pm 3\sigma_R\) (on the log scale).
\(\sigma_R\) and \(\rho\) are calculated for each OM from its historical recruitment deviations, estimated in the corresponding SS3 run, where \(\sigma_R\) is the standard deviation and \(\rho\) the lag-1 autocorrelation of the log recruitment deviations (Table 3.3).
Only the years in which the recruitment deviations are informed by the data are used (1996–2020), because the deviations in the early and final years are shrunk toward zero and would underestimate the variability.
The resulting \(\sigma_R\) (0.17 in the base case) is lower than the value assumed in the assessment (0.42), so the projected recruitment is less variable than the assessment’s prior assumption.

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.4 Observation Error for Simulated Data
The data used by the CMPs (catches and CPUE indices) are simulated from the OM with multiplicative observation error.
For catch, the observation error is conditioned on the historical fit between the OM catch and the catch data. The catch in the OMs matches the catch data closely (Section 2.1), so the catch data provided to the CMPs match the catches in the OM.
For the CPUE indices, the observation error is conditioned on the residuals between the observed index and the corresponding vulnerable abundance in the OM, including the lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals. The index observation error in the projection period follows the same truncated, autocorrelated log-normal process described above for the recruitment deviations, continuing from the last historical residual. All indices are assumed to be proportional to vulnerable abundance (i.e., no hyperstability or hyperdepletion).
Indices are simulated in the projection period only if they have data at the end of the historical period. Table 3.4 shows the standard deviation and lag-1 autocorrelation of the observation error for these indices in the base case OM. The conditioned values vary among the OMs, since each OM is conditioned on its own historical fit.

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.5 Unfished Spawning Biomass
Stock status, the limit reference point (LRP), and the threshold reference points of the HCRs are defined relative to the equilibrium unfished spawning biomass (\(SB_0\)), the spawning biomass of the unfished stock at equilibrium with average recruitment (\(R_0\)). The life-history parameters of the OMs do not change over time, so \(SB_0\) is constant over the historical and projection periods in each OM (it varies by less than 0.2% between the quarters of a year).
The dynamic unfished spawning biomass (\(SB_{F=0}\), the spawning biomass in the absence of fishing given the historical recruitment) was not used. The assessment starts from a fished state (an initial equilibrium fishing mortality), so \(SB/SB_{F=0}\) is sensitive to how the unfished trajectory is initialised in the early years. After about 1990, \(SB/SB_0\) is about 3% lower than \(SB/SB_{F=0}\) in all OMs.

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
4.1 Management Objectives
The CMPs are evaluated against the following management objectives (Table 4.1):
The CMPs are tuned in the base case OM to maximise the mean annual catch subject to the Safety objective (probability of at least 0.8) and the Status objective (probability of at least 0.5; Section 5.7). The Stability and Yield metrics are not used in the tuning; the trade-off between TAC stability and catch is shown by the variants of each CMP type with different limits on the change in the TAC.

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
Safety: Maintain spawning biomass above the limit reference point (LRP; 0.17\(SB_0\)) with at least 80% probability. A simulation in which spawning biomass falls below the LRP in any year of the evaluation period is considered a breach.
Status: Maintain fishing mortality at or below the target value (F\(_{40\%}\)) with at least 50% probability.
Stability: Changes in the TAC between management periods should be relatively gradual. This is measured by the probability that the TAC changes by no more than 10% between consecutive management periods, and by the probability of no management change (the TAC changes by no more than 1%; the CMPs leave the TAC unchanged when the change would be less than 1%).
Yield: Maintain catches above the average historical catch level, measured by the probability that the annual catch is at least the mean catch in 2008–2010. The mean annual catch is also reported.

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
4.3 Secondary Performance Metrics
Average TAC variability: the mean absolute relative change in the TAC between management cycles:
\[
\text{AAVY} = \frac{1}{S N_C} \sum_{s} \sum_{c} \Delta_{s,c}
\]
Kobe green quadrant: the probability that the stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring:
\[
P_{\text{Kobe}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(\frac{SB_{s,y}}{SB_{\text{MSY}}} > 1 \ \text{and} \ \frac{F_{s,y}}{F_{\text{MSY}}} < 1\right)
\]

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.1 Harvest Control Rules
The MSE currently includes three types of candidate management procedures (CMPs):
Each CMP type uses one of 3 harvest control rules (HCRs; Section 5.1), selected for that type together with its other settings (Section 5.7).
The variants of each type differ in the limit on the change in the TAC between management cycles (10%, 20%, 40%), for a total of 9 CMPs, which show the trade-off between TAC stability and catch.
Each CMP is named by its type, HCR, and TAC change limit; e.g., IR_H2_20 is the Index Rate CMP with HCR 2 and a 20% limit on the change in the TAC.
All CMPs set a single TAC for the total catch (removals, in t) of all fleets. The CMPs use data aggregated to calendar years: annual catches (summed over the quarters) and annual indices (averaged over the quarters with data).
The candidate HCRs (Table 5.1) were specified in terms of stock status, \(SB_{\text{current}}/SB_0\), where \(SB_0\) is the equilibrium unfished spawning biomass, and fishing mortality. Below the limit reference point (LRP), fishing mortality is reduced to a minimum level, \(F_{\text{min}}\); between the LRP and the threshold reference point (ThRP), it increases linearly to the target, \(F_{\text{TARGET}}\); and above the ThRP it is constant at the target. \(F_{X\%}\) is the fishing mortality that reduces the spawning potential ratio to \(X\%\).
The CMPs use the shape of these HCRs, but they do not set fishing mortality directly:
The fishing mortality that results in the OM therefore depends on how well the TAC matches the true state of the stock, and can differ from the fishing intensity intended by the HCR.
The HCR multiplier for each CMP type is (Figure 5.1):
The minimum multiplier is lower for the Index Target CMPs because their multiplier applies to a catch rather than to a fishing intensity. Above the ThRP, the Index Target CMPs keep the catch constant rather than the fishing intensity, so the fishing intensity decreases as the stock increases.

Stock status is estimated, not known. The CMPs do not observe spawning biomass, \(SB_0\), or fishing mortality. Stock status is estimated from the indices of abundance (Index Rate and Index Target) or from a surplus production model (Surplus Production; Section 5.2), and the control points are applied to this estimate.

The HCR sets a multiplier, not an F. The output of the HCR is a multiplier on a quantity specific to each CMP type, from which the TAC is calculated: the catch/index rate (Index Rate), a reference catch (Index Target), or a multiple of the \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) estimated by the surplus production model (Surplus Production). Only the Surplus Production CMPs estimate reference points, and these estimates are uncertain (Section 5.5).

The level of fishing is set by tuning. The fishing intensity above the ThRP is set by the tuning parameter (Section 5.7). The selected HCR for each CMP type is the one that gives the highest catch when tuned (step 1 in Section 5.7).

\(F_{\text{min}}\) is a relative reduction. At and below the LRP, the fishing intensity is reduced to \(F_{90\%}/F_{40\%}\) = 0.1 of its level above the ThRP, the ratio of \(F_{\text{min}}\) to \(F_{\text{TARGET}}\) from the per-recruit analysis of the base case OM in the terminal year of the assessment.





Index Rate and Surplus Production: the fishing intensity (the catch/index rate, or \(F\) relative to the estimated \(F_{\text{MSY}}\)) is multiplied by 0.1 at and below the LRP, increases linearly to 1 at the ThRP, and is 1 above the ThRP.

Index Target: the catch is constant above the ThRP, and decreases linearly to 0.1 \(\times\) LRP/ThRP of that catch at the LRP (Table 5.2).

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.2 Estimated Stock Status
The index-based CMPs estimate stock status from the two Japanese longline indices (S2 and S4; Section 2.1). Each index is expressed relative to its level at \(SB_0\), \(I_{0,j}\), calculated from the mean index over 2017–2021 and the mean \(SB/SB_0\) over the same years in the Base Case OM (0.345):
\[
I_{0,j} = \frac{\bar{I}_{j}}{\overline{SB/SB_0}}
\]
giving \(I_0\) = 1.47 and 0.846 for S2 and S4 respectively.
The current status of each index, \(S_j\), is the index averaged over the most recent years, after optional loess smoothing (the number of years and the smoothing are CMP settings; Section 5.7).
The estimated stock status is the mean of the two indices’ status relative to their \(I_0\):
\[
x = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{2} \frac{S_j}{I_{0,j}}
\]
The Surplus Production CMPs estimate stock status as the estimated biomass relative to carrying capacity (\(B/K\)) at the start of the year the TAC applies. The control points are specified in units of \(B/B_{\text{MSY}}\) by dividing the LRP and ThRP by \(B_{\text{MSY}}/K\), which depends on the shape of the production function (Section 5.5).

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.3 Index Rate
The Index Rate CMPs set the TAC as a catch/index rate multiplied by the current index. Each index is calibrated into its own catch/index rate, \(\hat{r}_j\): the mean total catch over the last 2 historical years divided by the mean of index \(j\) over the same years. The trial TAC is:
\[
\text{TrialTAC} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{2} S_j \times m \times \hat{r}_j \times \theta(x)
\]
where \(m\) is the tuning parameter and \(\theta(x)\) is the HCR multiplier (Figure 5.1):
\[
\theta(x) =
\begin{cases}
\phi & x \le \text{LRP} \\[4pt]
\phi + (1 - \phi)\dfrac{x - \text{LRP}}{\text{ThRP} - \text{LRP}} & \text{LRP} < x < \text{ThRP} \\[4pt]
1 & x \ge \text{ThRP}
\end{cases}
\]
with \(\phi = F_{\text{min}}/F_{\text{TARGET}}\) = 0.1. Because the catch/index rate is calibrated to the recent catch, \(m\) = 1 corresponds to the recent catch/index ratio.
The Index Rate CMPs use HCR 1 (ThRP = 35% \(SB_0\)), with current status calculated from the index averaged over the most recent year after loess smoothing (Section 5.7).

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.4 Index Target
The Index Target CMPs set the TAC as a reference catch, the mean total catch over the last 5 historical years (\(\bar{C}\)), scaled by the tuning parameter and the HCR:
\[
\text{TrialTAC} = m \times \bar{C} \times \theta_C(x)
\]
where \(\theta_C(x)\) has the same shape as \(\theta(x)\), with \(\phi\) = 0.1 \(\times\) LRP/ThRP (Figure 5.1). The TAC is therefore constant above the ThRP, so the catch does not increase when the stock is above the ThRP.
The Index Target CMPs use HCR 1 (ThRP = 35% \(SB_0\)), with current status calculated from the index averaged over the most recent year after loess smoothing (Section 5.7).

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.5 Surplus Production
The Surplus Production CMPs fit a Schaefer surplus production model (Pella and Tomlinson 1969) to the annual catch and the four Japanese longline indices (S1–S4), each with its own catchability. \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) and MSY are estimated, and the stock is assumed to be unfished at the start of the catch series (1975).
In each management cycle, the model is fitted to the available data and projected to the start of the year the TAC applies, assuming the catch in the intervening years is the TAC in force. The fishing mortality is:
\[
F = m \times \hat{F}_{\text{MSY}} \times \theta\!\left(\hat{B}/\hat{K}\right)
\]
where \(m\) is the tuning parameter and \(\theta\) is the HCR multiplier (Figure 5.1). The TAC is the mean annual catch when the model is projected at \(F\) over the 3-year management cycle. If the model fit fails or does not converge, the previous TAC is kept.
The Surplus Production CMPs use HCR 1 (ThRP = 35% \(SB_0\)) (Section 5.7).






WarningModel convergence



In the projections, the surplus production model failed to converge in 46–60% of the management cycles, depending on the OM, so the previous TAC was kept in these cycles. In 10–20% of the simulations, the model did not converge in any management cycle, so the TAC remained at its initial level throughout the projection period.
The results for the Surplus Production CMPs are therefore largely determined by how the TAC is set when the model fails, rather than by the model estimates, and should not be considered further without additional analysis of the model fits.

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.6 TAC Change Limits
For all CMPs, the proportional change from the previous TAC is limited to 10%, 20%, 40%, both up and down, and changes smaller than 1% leave the TAC unchanged:
\[
\text{TAC} = \text{TAC}_{\text{prev}} \times \min\left(\max\left(\frac{\text{TrialTAC}}{\text{TAC}_{\text{prev}}},\ 1 - \delta\right),\ 1 + \delta\right)
\]
where \(\delta\) is the TAC change limit and \(\text{TAC}_{\text{prev}}\) is the TAC in force.

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.7 Tuning Methodology
Each CMP has a single tuning parameter, \(m\), that scales the target fishing intensity: the catch/index rate (Index Rate), the reference catch (Index Target), or \(F\) relative to \(\hat{F}_{\text{MSY}}\) (Surplus Production).
The CMPs are tuned for the Base Case OM to maximise the mean annual catch over 2028–2057, subject to the Safety and Status objectives (Chapter 4):


Safety: the probability that spawning biomass remains above the LRP in every year is at least 0.8;

Status: the probability that \(F \leq F_{40\%}\) is at least 0.5.

The tuning is done in two steps.

5.7.1 Step 1: CMP Settings
The HCR and the other settings of each CMP type were selected from a set of candidate values (Table 5.3):

Each configuration was projected at 5 values of \(m\) over 0.25–4, using the first 50 simulations, and the catch at the largest value of \(m\) that meets both constraints was interpolated.
The 2 configurations with the highest catch were then fully tuned (Step 2) on all simulations, and the configuration with the highest catch was selected.

The selected HCR and settings were then used for all CMPs of that type.
The settings include the HCR (Table 5.1), the number of recent years the index is averaged over to calculate current status, whether the index is smoothed (loess) before calculating its status, and the shape parameter of the surplus production model. The calibration period of the Index Rate and Index Target CMPs was not included, because it only scales the catch/index rate or the reference catch, which is also scaled by \(m\).

5.7.2 Step 2: Tuning Parameter
\(m\) was then tuned for each of the 9 CMPs. It was first evaluated on a grid of 7 log-spaced values over 0.25–4, which was extended if necessary, and then refined towards the largest value that meets both constraints (or the value with the highest catch, if that is lower), until the range of \(m\) is within 1% or the binding constraint is within 0.5% of its minimum.
For each CMP type, the smallest TAC change limit (10%) gives the most stable TAC, and is always retained. A larger limit is retained only if it increases the mean catch by at least 2% compared with the next smaller retained limit, so the retained CMPs show the trade-off between TAC stability and catch. title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
4.2 Calculation of the Performance Indicators
All performance indicators are calculated over the 30 years in which the CMPs set the TAC (2028–2057), for each OM and CMP. The following notation is used:


\(s = 1, \ldots, S\) indexes the simulations and \(y \in \mathcal{Y}\) the \(N_Y\) = 30 years;

\(B_{s,y}\) is the annual spawning biomass relative to \(SB_0\): the mean over the quarters of year \(y\) of the female spawning biomass relative to \(SB_0\), the equilibrium unfished spawning biomass, which is constant over time (it varies by less than 0.2% between the quarters of a year);

\(F_{s,y}\) is the annual apical fishing mortality. Fishing mortality is an instantaneous rate per quarter, so \(F_{s,y}\) is the sum over the quarters; because \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) and \(F_{\text{target}}\) are the same in every quarter, the annual ratios \(F_{s,y}/F_{\text{MSY}}\) and \(F_{s,y}/F_{\text{target}}\) are the means of the quarterly ratios;

\(C_{s,y}\) is the annual catch (total removals of all fleets, in t), summed over the quarters;

\(\text{TAC}_{s,c}\) is the TAC set in management cycle \(c = 1, \ldots, N_C\), and \(\Delta_{s,c} = \lvert \text{TAC}_{s,c} - \text{TAC}_{s,c-1} \rvert / \text{TAC}_{s,c-1}\) is the relative change in the TAC;

\(\mathrm{I}(\cdot)\) is 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise.

Probabilities are calculated for each simulation and averaged over the simulations. When a performance indicator is calculated for a set of OMs, it is averaged over the simulations of all OMs in the set.

4.2.1 Indicators of the Candidate Management Objectives
Safety: the probability that spawning biomass remains above the LRP in every year:
\[
P_{\text{Safety}} = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s} \mathrm{I}\left(\min_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} B_{s,y} > 0.17\right)
\]
Status: the probability that fishing mortality is at or below the F target, and the median ratio of the F target to fishing mortality:
\[
P_{\text{Status}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(F_{s,y} \leq F_{\text{target}}\right)
\]
\[
\frac{F_{\text{target}}}{F} = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s} \operatorname*{median}_{y} \left(\frac{F_{\text{target}}}{F_{s,y}}\right)
\]
where \(F_{\text{target}}\) is F\(_{40\%}\), the apical fishing mortality that reduces the female spawning potential ratio to 40%. \(F_{s,y}/F_{\text{target}}\) is calculated from \(F_{s,y}/F_{\text{MSY}}\) and the ratio of \(F_{\text{target}}\) to \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) in the terminal year of the assessment in each OM.
Stability: the probability that the TAC changes by no more than 10% between management cycles, and the probability of no management change, i.e. that spawning biomass is above the threshold reference point (ThRP) of the CMP’s HCR:
\[
P_{\text{Stability}} = \frac{1}{S N_C} \sum_{s} \sum_{c} \mathrm{I}\left(\Delta_{s,c} \leq 0.1\right)
\]
\[
P_{\text{No change}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(B_{s,y} > \text{ThRP}\right)
\]
Yield: the probability that the annual catch is at least the mean historical catch in 2008–2010 (\(\bar{C}_{\text{ref}}\), in the OM), and the mean annual catch:
\[
P_{\text{Yield}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(C_{s,y} \geq \bar{C}_{\text{ref}}\right)
\]
\[
\bar{C} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} C_{s,y}
\]

4.2.2 Other Performance Indicators
Safety (proportion of years): the probability that spawning biomass is above the LRP, over all years:
\[
P_{\text{Safety,years}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(B_{s,y} > 0.17\right)
\]
Average TAC variability: the mean absolute relative change in the TAC between management cycles:
\[
\text{AAVY} = \frac{1}{S N_C} \sum_{s} \sum_{c} \Delta_{s,c}
\]
Kobe green quadrant: the probability that the stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring:
\[
P_{\text{Kobe}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(\frac{SB_{s,y}}{SB_{\text{MSY}}} > 1 \ \text{and} \ \frac{F_{s,y}}{F_{\text{MSY}}} < 1\right)
\]

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
Safety: Maintain spawning biomass above the limit reference point (LRP; 0.17\(SB_0\)) with at least 80% probability. A simulation in which spawning biomass falls below the LRP in any year of the evaluation period is considered a breach.
Status: Maintain fishing mortality at or below the target value (F\(_{40\%}\)) with at least 50% probability.
Stability: Changes in the TAC between management periods should be relatively gradual. This is measured by the probability that the TAC changes by no more than 10% between consecutive management periods, and by the probability of no management change (the TAC changes by no more than 1%; the CMPs leave the TAC unchanged when the change would be less than 1%).
Yield: Maintain catches above the average historical catch level, measured by the probability that the annual catch is at least the mean catch in 2008–2010. The mean annual catch is also reported.
